analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps from $5.15 to $7.25 an hour.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 315-116 and the Senate 94-3; the federal minimum wage rose in three steps to $7.25 an hour and the bill became law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill raises the federal minimum wage in three steps — to $5.85 an hour within about two months, $6.55 a year later, and $7.25 two years after that. It also applies the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands, starting at $3.55 there and rising 50 cents every six months until it matches the federal level. To win Senate approval, a second title was added with a package of tax breaks for small businesses, including extended equipment expensing, faster depreciation for restaurant and retail improvements, easier cash accounting, and hiring tax credits.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid less than the new minimum, whose hourly pay rises in three scheduled steps over two years [S2][S4]. It also extends federal wage protections to workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, whose local minimum wage starts far below the federal level and climbs toward it [S3][S4]. Small businesses gain from the tax title: extended expensing of assets through 2010, 15-year depreciation for leasehold, restaurant, and retail improvements, cash accounting for firms with up to $10 million in receipts, and a work opportunity tax credit extended through 2012 with larger credits for hiring disabled veterans [S4].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.85 an hour beginning 60 days after enactment, $6.55 twelve months later, and $7.25 twenty-four months later [S2][S4].
Applies federal minimum wage requirements to the Northern Mariana Islands, raising that Commonwealth's minimum from $3.55 by 50 cents every six months until it reaches the federal wage [S3][S4].
Extends the combined work opportunity and welfare-to-work tax credit through 2012 and increases the countable wages for disabled veterans from $6,000 to $12,000 [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that pay minimum wage — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other small employers — bear higher payroll costs as the wage floor rises [S2]. The tax title offsets part of that cost for small businesses but reduces federal revenue, partly balanced by new revenue provisions such as taxing wealthy people who give up U.S. citizenship to avoid taxes, denying deductions for punitive damages and government fines, and doubling penalties on offshore tax shelters [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Businesses paying minimum wage, mostly small employers

drawbacks.text: The increase is phased in over two years, so workers at the bottom wait up to 24 months for the full $7.25 [S2][S4].

The Senate version carries a package of business tax breaks — extended expensing, accelerated depreciation, doubled cash-accounting eligibility, and hiring credits — that reduces federal revenue [S4].
Employers paying the new minimum face higher labor costs, which economists warn can be passed to customers or reduce hiring at the lowest rungs — the trade-off every minimum wage increase carries.

In the Northern Mariana Islands, the transition keeps the local minimum at $3.55 initially and lets it rise only 50 cents every six months, leaving island workers below the federal wage for years [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and large: the lowest-paid workers get a higher wage floor, the first mechanism Congress has for lifting pay at the bottom. The main costs fall on the employers who pay those wages, and the Senate's answer was to sweeten the bill with small business tax breaks rather than absorb the cost publicly — a real price in revenue, though partly offset by revenue provisions aimed at tax avoidance. The slow two-year phase-in and the long transition in the Northern Mariana Islands blunt the benefit but do not change the overall balance: this is a bill whose main effect is a pay raise for low-wage workers.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it overwhelmingly, Senate Republicans first blocked a final vote, but after a small-business tax title was added the Senate passed it 94-3 and the bill became law.

narrative.text: Introduced January 5, 2007, and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S7].

On January 10 the House defeated a Republican motion to recommit — which would have added a minimum-wage provision tied to employer health benefits — 287-144, with all 233 voting Democrats against it [S9].
The House passed the bill 315-116: all 233 voting Democrats in favor, 82 of 202 Republicans in favor [S8].
The Senate's first cloture vote — a procedural vote needing 60 senators to allow a final vote — failed 54-43, with 47 of 49 Democrats in favor but only 5 of 49 Republicans [S11].
After a second title of small business tax provisions was added, cloture was invoked 88-8, with 39 Republicans joining all Democrats [S12].
The Senate passed the amended bill 94-3 on February 1, 2007, with 45 of 49 Republicans in favor [S13].
The bill became law, with the wage increases and the small business tax title intact [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage workers, who gained a rising federal wage floor through $7.25 an hour, and small businesses, which received a package of tax incentives in exchange for the higher wage costs.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply: all 233 voting Democrats yes versus 82 of 202 Republicans. In the Senate, the first cloture vote failed along party lines (Democrats 47-0 in favor, Republicans 5-43), but after tax provisions for small business were added, 39 Republicans joined cloture and the bill passed 94-3.

industries.industry: Small businesses and other minimum-wage employers
industries.note: They must pay a rising wage floor, the direct cost of the bill. The Senate version offsets part of that with extended equipment expensing, faster depreciation, easier cash accounting, and hiring credits [S4].

The tax title creates a new federal certification regime under which these payroll firms are treated as the employer for employment taxes, with bond and audit requirements — establishing their role in law [S5].

industries.industry: Owners of S corporations and banks
industries.note: The tax title loosens S corporation rules, excluding capital gains from passive investment income limits and easing treatment of bank director stock and bank conversions to S corporation status [S4].
New rules tax expatriates as if they sold their property the day before giving up citizenship, with only a $600,000 exclusion, and can bar reentry for noncompliance [S4].

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands employers (garment and tourism)
industries.note: Federal minimum wage now applies, starting at $3.55 and rising 50 cents every six months toward the federal level — a long transition that phases in the cost gradually [S3][S4].
